amendments.rule: **A verbless clause with a prepositional predicate takes its supplied copula on the preposition.** Rule 20 supplies the copula from the construction; where the predicate is a prepositional phrase, the copula joins the preposition heading that phrase and the unit heads on the preposition — `בְכַפֵּיהֶם` → *is in their hands*, `בִמְסִלּוֹתָם` → *are in their paths*, `אִתָּנוּ` → *are with us*, `עָלֶיךָ` → *is upon thee*. **A resultative prepositional predicate takes the ASV's supplied result or change frame on the same terms.** The preposition carries the relation that English expresses with the frame: `לְ` → *to be*, *shall be turned into*, *will be unto*, or *shalt become*. This is not rule 20's wholly supplied lexical verb, because removing the English frame removes the preposition's own result relation; any explicit Hebrew subject still takes the English subject pronoun separately. Head the preposition's unit on the English word carrying that relation — *to* in *to be*, *into* in *shall be turned into*, *unto* in *will be unto*, and *become* where no English preposition remains. The ordinary copular case is settled rather than a tie: the corpus reads it this way in 103 units across 39 chapters and never moves the copula onto the object noun instead. It is settled; the note need not hedge it. **A relational verb the ASV writes where a copula would stand goes the same way.** Where a possessive or belonging `לְ` heads the predicate and the ASV renders the clause with a verb of belonging rather than a bare copula — `אֲשֶׁר לַבָּיִת` → *which belonged to the house* — that verb is part of the preposition's own rendering and joins its unit, headed on the English preposition written for it. It is not rule 20's wholly supplied lexical verb: drop the verb and the preposition's relation is what has gone and nothing else, which is the subtraction test rule 43 applies to the same clause written with *had*. Where the ASV does write *had* or *have*, rule 43 governs; where it writes a bare copula, the first sentence of this rule does. **But every sentence above governs a phrase for which the ASV has written an English preposition, and says nothing about one for which it has written none.** Where the ASV spends no word on the preposition's own relation and instead writes that relation inside the following word — a possessive or belonging `לְ` rendered as an English genitive, `לַיהוָה` → *is Jehovah's* — rule 30's one-rendering condition is met: one English word carries both the relation and the lexeme, and the preposition shares that word's unit, headed on the word carrying the lexeme. The construction's copula then joins that one fused unit, exactly as it joins `לִפְנֵי` → *was before* under rule 30, which states that a copula the construction hands to the whole of an expression does not defeat the condition. Test by the subtraction rules 16, 30 and 43 use: drop the copula and ask whether the preposition has lost a rendering of its own or only the clause has lost the tense English writes for it. Where only the clause is diminished, the preposition has no separate English and fuses; where an English preposition of its own remains — *is in their hands* — the first sentence of this rule governs and the copula stays with it. Do not reach for rule 2 to split the fused pair on the ground that the noun or name holds an English word of its own: that reasoning is rule 57's, where each of two nouns holds a word, and here the preposition holds none. The corpus reads `לְ` + the divine name this way in six units across five chapters — *is Jehovah's*, *shall be Jehovah's*, *am Jehovah's*, and a bare *Jehovah's* — and never splits a copula onto the preposition beside a separately aligned name. **And every sentence above governs a preposition that is itself the clause's predicate, never one heading an adjunct the ASV has merely placed the copula beside.** Where a nominal predicate stands in the verbless clause and a prepositional phrase modifies it, the copula and any dummy subject are rule 20's and join that nominal, whichever order the ASV writes the two in: `חֻקַּת עוֹלָם לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם` → *it shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations* and `מֵאֵת בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּרִית עוֹלָם` → *it is on the behalf of the children of Israel an everlasting covenant* are one construction, and both give the copula to the construct nominal, the second unit discontinuous around the fronted phrase under rule 25 while the preposition keeps only the English written for its own relation. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, exactly as rule 20 directs, since a phrase the ASV fronts puts the copula beside something that predicates nothing; and do not let a fused compound preposition draw the copula in under rule 30's one-rendering condition, which reaches a copula the construction hands to that expression and not one another morpheme is there to take. Where the clause writes no nominal predicate at all, nothing competes and the first sentence of this rule governs as before.
amendments.why: Rule 49's first sentence is conditioned on the prepositional phrase being the predicate, but the rule nowhere considers a clause that also writes a nominal predicate, and nowhere says what to do when the ASV fronts the adjunct so that the copula falls beside it. LEV.24.8 was aligned under rule 49 on exactly that reasoning, against LEV.24.3, which takes the same shape the other way. The amendment states the boundary and the discontinuity the corrected reading requires, and adds the one further trap the verse pass fell into: a rule-30 fusion sitting where the copula falls does not thereby earn it. It narrows rather than widens, so it contradicts none of the 103 corpus units rule 49 already cites, all of which are genuine prepositional predicates.

conventions: Verbless clause with both a nominal predicate and a prepositional phrase: the construction-supplied copula and dummy subject go to the nominal, however the ASV orders the two. חֻקַּת עוֹלָם at v. 3 takes it shall be and בְּרִית עוֹלָם at v. 8 takes it is, the latter discontinuous around the fronted מֵאֵת בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל, which keeps only on the behalf of. Rule 49 was not applied to a preposition that heads an adjunct rather than the predicate.

מִחוּץ (לְ): the preposition and חוּץ are one fused unit under rule 30 whether the ASV writes without (vv. 3, 14) or out of (v. 23), headed on the token carrying the lexeme; the לְ that follows it and any אֶל standing before it are each their own unrepresented unit under rule 40, the one English rendering carrying the whole relation.

Casuistic אִישׁ with כִּי: the doubled contiguous formula אִישׁ אִישׁ כִּי rendered by the single word Whosoever (v. 15) is one fused unit under rule 30, headed on the first אִישׁ, with כִּי inside it because Whosoever carries the subordination as well as the distributive. Where the Hebrew writes a single אִישׁ and the ASV spends a word on each morpheme — he / that at v. 17, a man / if at v. 19 — rule 30's condition is unmet and rule 2 splits, אִישׁ taking the nominal word and כִּי the subordinator.

כַּגֵּר כָּאֶזְרָח rendered as well ... as (vv. 16, 22): the Hebrew writes a comparative preposition for each member, so this is not rule 14's correlative pair resting on one connective. The first כְּ takes the whole opening expression as well, headed on as, and the second takes the answering as. Where the ASV additionally writes a for before each noun (v. 22), that word is the noun's own under rule 33, the preposition having already spent its English.

report: One genuine cross-verse split: the verbless-clause copula. LEV.24.3 gives the supplied 'it shall be' to the predicate nominal חֻקַּת (rule 20); LEV.24.8 gives 'it is' to the adjunct preposition מֵאֵת under rule 49. Same construction — a construct nominal X עוֹלָם as predicate with a prepositional phrase beside it — and nothing in the source licenses the difference, only the ASV's fronting of the phrase. מֵאֵת בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל predicates nothing; בְּרִית עוֹלָם is the predicate.

LEV.24.8 patched: 'it is' moves onto בְּרִית, whose unit is discontinuous around the fronted phrase (rule 25); מֵאֵת keeps 'on the behalf of' and its head on 'behalf'. LEV.24.3 is the correct member of the pair and is left alone; no other verse in the chapter sets a nominal predicate against a competing prepositional phrase.

Checked and cleared as ASV-licensed rather than split: the waw to 'that' at vv. 2 and 7 against 'And' at v. 9; אִישׁ אִישׁ כִּי fused to 'Whosoever' at v. 15 against the split אִישׁ / כִּי at vv. 17 and 19 (doubled source and one English word against single source and two); מִחוּץ to 'without' (3, 14) and 'out of' (23), each headed on חוּץ with the following לְ and any preceding אֶל unrepresented; the article to 'each' (7), 'Every' (8), 'the', and unrepresented, each read off what the ASV writes where the phrase's the would stand; the two כְּ ... כְּ pairs (16, 22); עָרַךְ to 'keep'/'set in order' (3, 4, 8), all headed on 'order'; articular participles heading on 'him' (14, 23) against anarthrous ones heading on the verb (16, 18, 21).

The four added units, which the lemma-keyed table cannot see, were read against the whole dump: the italic 'of an ephah' (5) and 'of Jehovah' (16), the appositional 'even' (7) with no marker standing on the phrase it introduces, and the supplied object 'him' of 'that heard him' (14). Each is consistent with the others and with the chapter's practice of folding supplied determiners into their noun and supplied subject pronouns into their verb. No fifth supplied word was found folded in where these four were split off.

BSB: no genuine error. Every disagreement is a documented convention difference — the לְ of לֵאמֹר (rule 27), the לְ and אֶל around מִחוּץ and the בְּ of רָגַם בְּ (rule 40), unrendered article morphemes (rules 29, 47), and the doubled בְּיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת with the second יִהְיֶה of v. 22 (rule 22), where BSB attaches the morpheme to its own phrase. Nothing was changed to improve the rate.
